newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks applaud court ruling on Marcos money.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks applaud court ruling on Marcos money.

text.p: Swiss banks holding funds linked to late Philippine dictator Ferdinand Marcos applauded a U.S. court reversal of an earlier order to hand over the cash, but said it was only one step in a struggle that could drag on for years.
"We have accepted the court's unanamous decision with satisfaction," SBC spokesman Thomas Staffelbach, adding, "We will now review our position in light of this new development."

Various rival groups have staked claims to Marcos monies in Switzerland at Swiss Bank Corp and Credit Suisse. The two have an estimated $475 million deposited by the late dictator Marcos, who died in exile in Hawaii in 1989.
The internationally active banks, with legal costs mounting, would like nothing better than to settle the matter.
But they have been attempting to avoid court orders in different countries that could force them to pay multiple claims, in effect paying out the same money twice.

In this most recent decision, a U.S. Appeals Court in San Francisco, in a ruling released on Wednesday, said that a district judge in Los Angeles had no authority to order the banks to turn over the contested funds to court custody.
Under the Los Angeles judge's order issued last December, the money would have to be turned over to the U.S. court so that rival claims could be decided.
The two Swiss banks appealed that order.
"We are very happy about this ruling, but we stil have to wait and see what actions are taken by the other parties represented by Mr. Swift," Credit Suisse spokeswoman Seraina Conrad said.
Robert Swift is the lawyer representing nearly 10,000 human rights victims of the late Marcos's regime.
The claimants could decide to take an appeal to the highest court in the U.S. and such a move would mean that the legal wrangling in the U.S. is far from over.
The case in the U.S. stems from attempts by victims of the Marcos government to secure payment of a huge court judgment they won against the Marcos estate.

In 1994, a federal jury in a class action civil rights suit in Hawaii awarded $1.9 billion to 9,500 victims and family members of victims who suffered at the hands of Marcos's government, accused of major human rights abuses during his rule, which ended in 1986.
In another case in Switzerland, a Zurich district court is considering an appeal of an earlier court order to turn the money over to the Philippine government.

The Philippine government has argued that any money recovered from the banks belongs to the government because it was stolen from the national coffers. The Marcos family has been accused of stealing about $5 billion during the dictator's 20-year rule.
Negotiations had been held among the various parties to try to resolve the dispute over the competing claims but have so far failed to find a solution.
